name: Visual pathway
summary: Light falling on the retina is converted by photoreceptors, bipolar cells and ganglion cells into action potentials that leave the eye in the optic nerve. At the chiasm the fibers from the nasal retina (temporal field) cross so that each optic tract carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes to the lateral geniculate body. Geniculate neurons project as the optic radiation: fibers for the upper field loop forward into the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) and fibers for the lower field pass through the parietal lobe, all ending in the calcarine cortex with the macula at the pole. The pathway is the most precisely localizable in neurology: the shape of the field defect, its congruity, macular sparing and the pupils together give the level.

origin.note: Retinal ganglion cells (third-order neurons of the retina) form the optic nerve; the pathway is CNS from the retina onward.

neuronChain.synapse: lateral geniculate nucleus (also pretectum, superior colliculus, suprachiasmatic nucleus)
layer IV of the striate cortex via the optic radiation

decussation.note: Nasal retinal fibers (about 53%) cross; temporal fibers remain uncrossed.

waypoints.note: optic nerve from the disc through the optic canal
optic tract around the cerebral peduncle carrying the contralateral hemifield
six-layered relay; pupillary fibers leave before it
Meyer's loop through the temporal lobe (upper field)
striate cortex; macula at the pole

termination: Primary visual cortex lining the calcarine sulcus, with onward projection to extrastriate areas (V2–V5), the ventral stream (temporal) and the dorsal stream (parietal).

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Monocular loss (central scotoma, altitudinal or arcuate defects) with an RAPD and reduced acuity/color
Bitemporal hemianopia (or junctional scotoma); acuity preserved unless the nerves are involved
Incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia with a contralateral RAPD and later bow-tie optic atrophy
Congruous sectoranopia or quadrantic defects with normal pupils
Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia, often with neglect or asymmetric optokinetic nystagmus
Highly congruous contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing; pupils normal
Cortical blindness with normal pupils and, in Anton syndrome, denial

pearls: Monocular = in front of the chiasm; bitemporal = chiasm; homonymous = behind the chiasm, and the more congruous the more posterior
An RAPD localizes to the nerve, chiasm or tract; geniculate, radiation and cortical lesions spare the pupil
Macular sparing means occipital cortex with collateral MCA supply

somatotopy: Retinotopic throughout: upper retina (lower field) stays superior in the tract, radiation (parietal) and cortex (cuneus); lower retina (upper field) runs inferiorly (Meyer's loop, lingual gyrus); macula central in the nerve, posterior in the chiasm, occupying the occipital pole.
